entities.name: Khamudi
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Khamudi, the final Hyksos monarch of the Fifteenth Dynasty, presided over the northern portion of Egypt from his capital Avaris during a pivotal and brief reign, traditionally dated from 1541 or 1534 BCE to 1600 BCE. His rule marked the culmination of the Second Intermediate Period, an era defined by foreign domination and fragmented political authority within Egypt. Khamudi's significance lies not in his accomplishments, but in his role as the antagonist in the ultimate conflict for Egyptian reunification, pitting his Hyksos kingdom against the resurgent native Egyptian forces from Thebes.

His ascension to the throne followed the long and influential reign of Apophis, a period characterized by diplomatic overtures and intermittent conflicts with the Theban Seventeenth Dynasty. Khamudi inherited a kingdom under siege, as Ahmose I, founder of the Eighteenth Dynasty and the New Kingdom, systematically advanced northward. The climactic events of his reign included the siege and capture of Avaris around 1550 BCE, forcing Khamudi to flee. Following the fall of his capital, Ahmose pursued the retreating Hyksos forces into southern Canaan, besieging them for three years at the fortress of Sharuhen, a campaign that definitively dismantled Hyksos power and influence.

Khamudi's ultimate defeat at Sharuhen around 1600 BCE was more than just the end of a dynasty; it signaled the complete expulsion of the Hyksos from Egypt and the permanent reunification of the Two Lands under native Egyptian rule. This victory paved the way for the unparalleled prosperity, imperial expansion, and cultural flourishing of the New Kingdom, transforming Egypt into a dominant power in the ancient Near East. The memory of Khamudi and the Hyksos became a foundational narrative for the New Kingdom pharaohs, who frequently invoked their expulsion as a testament to their divine mandate and strength.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Khamudi's defeat marked the decisive end of Hyksos rule, leading directly to the reunification of Egypt under Ahmose I and the establishment of the powerful New Kingdom, a period of unprecedented imperial expansion and cultural zenith.
